facts.statement: Wulagasaurus is a genus of saurolophine hadrosaurid dinosaur named after its discovery locality in Heilongjiang, China.
facts.quote: Wulagasaurus (meaning "Wulaga lizard", in reference to the discovery locality) is a genus of saurolophine hadrosaurid dinosaur known from the Late Cretaceous of Heilongjiang, China.

facts.statement: Pascal Godefroit and colleagues named the genus Wulagasaurus in 2008.
facts.quote: Wulagasaurus was named by Pascal Godefroit and colleagues in 2008.

facts.statement: Only partial remains of Wulagasaurus are currently known.
facts.quote: Only partial remains are known at this time.

facts.statement: The only known species, W. dongi, was named in honor of the Chinese paleontologist Dong Zhiming.
facts.quote: The type and only species to date is W. dongi, named in honor of Chinese paleontologist Dong Zhiming.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Wulagasaurus is a partial dentary, which is the tooth-bearing bone of the lower jaw.
facts.quote: Wulagasaurus is based on GMH W184, a partial dentary (toothbearing bone of the lower jaw).

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Wulagasaurus was the most basal known saurolophine, providing evidence that saurolophines and hadrosaurids likely originated in Asia.
facts.quote: Godefroit and colleagues performed a phylogenetic analysis that suggests Wulagasaurus was the most basal saurolophine known (which would result in a long ghost lineage), and interpreted this as evidence that saurolophines and hadrosaurids in general originated in Asia, which has been supported by other finds since.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated Wulagasaurus to be 9 meters long and weigh 3 tonnes in 2010.
facts.quote: In 2010 Gregory S. Paul estimated its size at 9 meters (30 ft) and 3 tonnes (3.3 short tons).

facts.statement: As a hadrosaurid, Wulagasaurus was an herbivore.
facts.quote: As a hadrosaurid, Wulagasaurus would have been an herbivore.

facts.statement: As a hadrosaurid, Wulagasaurus was an herbivore that walked by alternating between bipedal and quadrupedal positions.
facts.quote: Como hadrosáurido, Wulagasaurus habría sido un herbívoro que caminaba alternando la posición bípeda con la cuadrúpeda.

facts.statement: Remains of Wulagasaurus were found in a bonebed dominated by the lambeosaurine hadrosaurid Sahaliyania in the Yuliangze Formation of Heilongjiang, China.
facts.quote: Su restos fueron encontrados en Heilongjiang, China, en una cama de huesos dominada por restos del hadrosáurido lambeosaurino Sahaliyania en la Formación Yuliangze del Maastrichtiano medio, que data de hace 69 millones de años.

facts.statement: Wulagasaurus is classified within the family Hadrosauridae.
Wulagasaurus belongs to the subfamily Saurolophinae.
Wulagasaurus lived during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Fossils of Wulagasaurus were found in the middle Maastrichtian-age Yuliangze Formation, dated to 69 million years ago.
rejected.quote: Its remains were found in a bonebed in the middle Maastrichtian-age Yuliangze Formation, dated to 69 million years ago.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'Yuliangze Formation dated to 69 million years ago'

rejected.statement: Wulagasaurus is distinguished from other hadrosaurids by its slender dentary and a unique upper arm structure with distinctive muscle attachment sites.
rejected.quote: It can be distinguished from other hadrosaurids by its slender dentary and the unique form of its upper arm, which had distinctive articulations and placements for muscle attachments.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'distinguished from other hadrosaurids by its slender dentary'

rejected.statement: A 2012 study concluded that Wulagasaurus shared morphological similarities with Brachylophosaurus and Maiasaura, possibly forming a sub-clade within Brachylophosaurini.
rejected.quote: Based on both original and assigned specimens, they concluded that Wulagasaurus shared many morphological similarities with North American taxon's Brachylophosaurus and Maiasaura, possibly forming a clade-structure within the already existing clade Brachylophosaurini.
